Singapore
A Trip to the Future
From its immersive airport art to its hyperengineered skyline, the urban state offers a sci-fi vision for the present day. Photographs by Matthew Pillsbury / Text by Rachel Monroe
The Mirror Maze in Jewel Changi Airport was designed by the puzzlemaker Adrian Fisher, who also created the airport’s hedge maze.
The Rain Vortex, in the Jewel, is the world’s tallest indoor waterfall, at 130 feet.
Depictions of the future, whether dystopian or utopian, skew to the aggressively artificial: fluorescing cityscapes, interiors gleaming with stainless steel. Singapore, the tiny ultramodern city-state, advances another interpretation, one that has spawned one of the world’s biggest glass greenhouses, a grove of hundred-foot-tall futuristic “supertrees” that mimic photosynthesis with photovoltaic cells (at night, the branches emit a neon glow) and the world’s largest rooftop infinity pool. This is the future as hyperreal and lushly disorienting, a pseudonatural vision of the 21st century.
The Rain Vortex, in the Jewel, is the world’s tallest indoor waterfall, at 130 feet.
The latest incarnation is the Jewel, which opened at Changi Airport this spring and is billed as a “multidimensional retail journey that is set against a garden backdrop.” The bundt-cake-shaped structure glows invitingly between the airport’s terminals, on top of what was once a parking lot. The architect, Moshe Safdie, was inspired by the psychedelically verdant worlds in “Avatar” when conceiving the glass-and-metal building, a fitting habitat for beautiful, branded environments. World travelers wander through the Jewel’s two mazes (one made of hedges, the other of mirrors) or exercise their legs with a stroll across the Manulife Skynets, a mesh walkway stretched more than 80 feet in the air. Its centerpiece is the HSBC Rain Vortex, a cascade of rainwater that pours through an oculus in the roof and plummets 130 feet into a basement tank. It is the largest indoor waterfall in the world; at night, it’s the backdrop to a light-and-sound show. Encircling the Vortex is the Shiseido Forest Valley, a four-story terraced garden with thousands of plants from around the world.
It makes a bleak kind of sense that a country waging an existential battle against rising sea levels would come up with fantastical approximations of nature. As for what it’s like for visitors, the photographs of Matthew Pillsbury offer a clue, while evoking the dreamy liminal state of travel. Individuals blur into one another as they move within these optimized and extravagant unnatural natural spaces, subsumed by the experiences and environments constructed for them. The blurred masses seem less substantial, less vivid, indeed less real than the mesmerizing, climate-controlled city they move within.
The infinity pool atop the Marina Bay Sands floats more than 600 feet above Singapore; it has become a famous selfie spot for resort guests.
The Cloud Forest at Gardens by the Bay is a 115-foot artificial mountain covered in non-artificial tropical vegetation.

2
Norway
Majesty on the Wing
Enormous and indefatigable, sea eagles turn their daily hunt into a thrilling display of aerial dominance. Photographs by Paolo Pellegrin / Text by Helen Macdonald
The white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla), a species of sea eagle, is the largest bird of prey in Norway and among the largest species of eagle in the world, with a wingspan of up to eight feet.
Herring gulls flock chaotically around the boat, dipping to alight briefly on the heads and hands of its passengers. They — the humans — are on a pilgrimage to see white-tailed eagles; the gulls are the voyage’s attendant spirits.
Sea eagles are among the largest eagles in the world. White-tailed eagles spend most of the day perched and at rest, often looking unprepossessingly disheveled, like figures in thick fur coats. Their plumage is dark brown, bleached pale in places to resemble gilded chain mail. Their eyes are deep-set, pale and calculating, and they are formidable hunters. They’ll grab sea ducks from the waves, use seabird colonies as supermarket shelves, steal prey from gulls and ospreys and feast on offal from abattoirs. Most of all they love to fish, and the shallow waters off the coast of Norway are perfect hunting grounds. This region has among the densest populations of sea eagles anywhere in the world, and tourists flock to witness the power and precision of their hunting flights, the eagles attracted to fish tossed from the sides of boats.
For a bird of their size — their wingspan can reach eight feet — they flap fast and decisively. Their descents are rapid unfoldings of exquisite angles and incidences, the pale leading edge of their wings gleaming against the humid gray of air and water. An eagle plucking a fish from the surface of the water, wings flaring, talons down-dropped, is a perfect opportunity for the photographer.
There is more than simply a picture in that moment. Sea eagles have had symbolic significance in many cultures: Neolithic people in the Orkney Islands interred eagle bones with their own; Roman artists cast exquisite bronze eagle figurines. But for centuries humans have also shot, trapped and poisoned these eagles, destroyed their nests in fear of them taking livestock, of stealing things that are ours. What these human pilgrims upon a dark sea are witnessing is a kind of redemption in those brief and perfect moments where the wildest world turns midair, descends, picks our small silver offering gently from the water and carries it to the skies.
Norway is home to roughly 20 percent of the world’s white-tailed eagle population.
Small fishing villages like Reine, in the Lofoten archipelago, double as outposts for the intrepid birder.
A group of Danish visitors training their long lenses on seabirds. Boats also often motor past harbor porpoises, gray seals and the occasional orca or pilot whale swimming in the fjord.
Ole Martin Dahle, a guide who ventures out with groups some 250 days a year, says he has a “special relationship with the birds.” He thinks of them as indicators of broader environmental health. “If birds are doing well, the people also are doing well,” he says.
Gulls in the fjords of the Flatanger archipelago near Lauvsnes, a fishing town south of the Arctic Circle. White-tailed eagles sometimes look for congregations of herring gulls while scavenging for food. More often, they steal the catch of unsuspecting otters, which are prevalent in the fjords.
The view from a guesthouse in Lauvsnes.
Visitors are dressed for the changing weather in Norway’s fjords and water temperatures that vary from the high 50s in summer to near-freezing in winter.
Herring gulls flocking behind a tour boat, looking for handouts.
The white-tailed eagle population in Norway hasn’t always been so robust. They were hunted aggressively until 1968, when protections helped their numbers rebound from several hundred breeding pairs to thousands of pairs today.

3
Virginia
Heads of State
150 miles south of Washington, a crumbling shrine to presidential history. Photographs by Hannah Price / Text by Mark Leibovich
The busts once housed in Presidents Park were created by the Houston sculptor David Adickes, who was inspired after a trip to Mount Rushmore.
All the presidents stand between 15 and 18 feet tall, with the exception of a miniature model of Barack Obama, which is about two feet tall.
After driving down from Washington to Croaker, Va., I was greeted at the foot of a dirt driveway by “No Trespassing” and “Do Not Enter” signs. Up the driveway, 50 or so people were gathered before a burly guy in flip-flops: John Plashal, a local storyteller and, today, tour guide. There’s only so much I can tell you about the whole experience, because this is private property and things get a little complicated with legal and liability concerns. Look for him on the internet, is all I can say.
“People love places that are falling down,” Plashal told the group. “And people really love being in places where they’re not supposed to be.”
The place in question is a ragged industrial field that has become the repository for 42 giant busts of American presidents, sculpted by an artist named David Adickes, each some 15 to 18 feet in height and eight to 10 tons in weight. They used to inhabit something called Presidents Park, in nearby Williamsburg, but after that place closed in 2010, the orphaned commanders in concrete were transported by flatbed to Croaker, about 12 miles away. The brief but treacherous journey left the heads in various states of disrepair. Bill Clinton is missing part of his right ear. Woodrow Wilson looks as though he has leprosy. Ronald Reagan might have been struck by lightning. Abraham Lincoln has a hole in the back of his skull — as if he needed one of those!
All the presidents stand between 15 and 18 feet tall, with the exception of a miniature model of Barack Obama, which is about two feet tall.
Following Plashal’s directions, I walked past dumpsters and cones and barrels and portapotties, dirt piles and construction equipment, two goats. Finally, arranged in rows amid the weeds and wildflowers and overgrown grass, there were the presidents. They loomed grand and vulnerable, stately and a bit sad. I kept stepping back to view them all together, as a stalwart institution that has seen better days.
The other explorers scattered, taking selfies, noting the sideburns on John Quincy Adams. “I think the fat one back there is Martin Van Buren,” I heard someone say. Wandering around, I could not help wondering what it was like here at night when the flesh-and-bloods like me had gone. I imagined the concrete presidents reminiscing, murmuring about the decaying state of themselves, and of things.

4
Borneo
Deep in the Darkness
Far beneath the rainforest floor, in a pair of remote national parks, lie some of the world’s oldest signs of human activity. Photographs by Olaf Otto Becker / Text by Jake Nevins
In 1966, an archaeological team lead by Tom and Barbara Harrisson excavated groups of bones that suggested this stretch of the Niah Caves, called Lobang Hangus, was used around 13,000 years ago for discarding the remains of hunted animals.
A stalactite formation known as the jellyfish inside Lang’s Cave in Gunung Mulu National Park.
Scientific expeditions have plumbed the vast limestone caves of Borneo ever since the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace began writing about them in the mid-1800s. The accounts by Wallace, who speculated about the possibility of discovering prehistoric human remains within the caves, inspired Britain’s Royal Society to help fund an expedition there in 1878. In the resulting report, Alfred Hart Everett describes finding pottery fragments, a neolithic stone ax head and the remains of people who had “already reached an advanced stage of civilization.” (As a result, he declared, “no light has been thrown on the origin of the human race.”)
A stalactite formation known as the jellyfish inside Lang’s Cave in Gunung Mulu National Park.
Less than a century later, however, archaeologists working in a different cave recovered a fragmentary human skull that appeared to date from the late Pleistocene Era. Last year, scientists who had explored yet another Borneo cave in 1996 determined that a red image of a four-legged creature — seemingly a banteng, a species of Southeast Asian cattle — is the oldest known figurative art in the world. It was hand-painted onto the limestone at least 40,000 years ago, according to estimates, or some 8,000 years before the famous pictures of rhinos and lions in the French cave Chauvet.
The island of Borneo is almost entirely divided between Indonesia, where the picture of the banteng was found in Lubang Jeriji Saleh Cave, and Malaysia, whose caves in Niah National Park and Gunung Mulu National Park are tourist destinations. The photographer Olaf Otto Becker visited both parks. Though he saw no relics of ancient humans, living things were abundant: cave crickets, crabs, cockroaches, spiders and black-nest swiftlets in burrows overhead. And of course, bats. As many as three million of them are thought to live in Gunung Mulu’s Deer Cave alone, the single largest cave passage in the world. “They are not very satisfied when you come into the cave with a bright flashlight,” Becker says. “They are very nervous.” At dusk, he got to see them leave en masse — another reminder of the wonders within the caves — on their nightly search for food. “The sky was filled with snakelike petals,” he says, “a never-ending bat cloud in the form of a snake.”
The Harrissons discovered the so-called Deep Skull, an anatomically modern human skull between 30,000 and 40,000 years old, in the Niah Great Cave in 1958. Its expanse — the entrance here is 500 feet high — and the light levels within made photography difficult. ‘‘It is so dark in the center of the caves that most of the tourists will fail to see what I captured with this photograph,’’ Becker says. ‘‘I like technical challenges like this.’’
Visitors climb 240 stairs to enter the Clearwater Cave in Gunung Mulu National Park.
The eastern opening of Lobang Hangus in the Great Cave Complex in Niah National Park.
Deer Cave, in Gunung Mulu National Park, is 486 feet high and 466 feet wide at its widest point. Because of the extremely low light in the cave, multiple exposures had to be composited to create this photo illustration.
A small water bottle hangs at the left side of this cave mouth in Gunung Mulu National Park. The local Iban people use them to collect fresh water.

5
Namibia
Bones in the Sand
In the hulking detritus of southwestern Africa’s Skeleton Coast, a sobering testament to civilizational impermanence. Photographs by Glenna Gordon / Text by Michael Finkel
The Otavi was transporting guano, to be used as fertilizer, from nearby Mercury Island when it ran aground in 1945. Its wreckage remains in Spencer Bay, which is almost completely untouched by humans but home to thousands of fur seals.
The Shawnee, an American vessel that wrecked on Feb. 16, 1976, sits in surf along the Skeleton Coast. Namibia’s coastline shifts so much that over the years the sands have most likely previously covered the wreck.
The Skeleton Coast of southwestern Africa offers an epic view of an elemental struggle: raw, churning ocean in an endless tug-of-war against the indomitable march of desert sand. The word “beautiful” may not come to mind when voyaging here, though the name itself suggests “beauty” is wrong somehow. The shoreline, partly preserved in a 6,300-square-mile national park, evokes a feeling perhaps better described as “sublime,” with all the attendant awe and grandeur and fear that the word implies.
There are, indeed, skeletons — whale bones, some from the old hunting days, strewn like plane wreckage, as well as the bludgeoned hulks of cargo ships and fishing boats, possibly more than a thousand of them, slain by a lethal combination of dense coastal fog and shallow rocky outcrops. It’s a place ruled by fur seals and seabirds and the hardy saber-horned antelopes known as oryxes. Wind sculpts the sand, monumentally — miles of ripples, mountains of scalloped dunes, a starfish the size of a voting district — all of it constantly shifting and morphing.
The Shawnee, an American vessel that wrecked on Feb. 16, 1976, sits in surf along the Skeleton Coast. Namibia’s coastline shifts so much that over the years the sands have most likely covered the wreck.
Travel here is often via small chartered airplanes, departing from towns that already seem perched at earth’s edge. Photographer Glenna Gordon ventured farther than most, at times hiring a helicopter to reach remote wrecks. I flew out of Walvis Bay, along with my family, buzzing over this seam between land and sea, feeling conflicted by the great expense I’d incurred to see such primal nothingness in a part of the world where there’s little wealth, rattled to my heart by the incomprehensible immensity.
If the Skeleton Coast sounds unwelcoming, it’s true. People don’t really belong here. I’d leapt continents, four-wheeled over washboard roads, hired bush planes — harnessing all I could of civilization’s might — only to arrive in an area that made me feel insignificant and helpless. Sometimes we need such a kick to the hubris to be reminded of the planet’s true balance of power. Witness the iron- and steel-hulled ships, subsumed by sand, crumbling into rusty flakes. Humans often believe we can bend the world to our will, that our reign will be permanent. The Skeleton Coast offers a simple and powerful rebuttal.
The Brazilian cargo ship Frotamerica crashed in 2013. The 35,000-ton vessel was unmanned when it broke loose from its mooring. The wreckage and oil pollution present a threat to wildlife along the Namibia coast.
These whale bones, near Sandwich Harbor, have migrated inland with shifting sands. Many whales washed up after World War II, but some skeletons that date from the 1800s are still visible as are, on occasion, human bones — presumably the remains of miners and sailors.
A sign, bleached by the sun, gives directions to no one in a part of the country that often feels deserted.
The Eduard Bohlen II crashed in 1909. Starting in 1891, the ship was used to bring mail from Germany to western Africa. Later, after war broke out between the Germans and Hereros, it became a prison ship. In peacetime, it was refurbished as a passenger vessel. It even found a use after it wrecked: as a home for diamond miners.
The Zeila, stranded on a rocky reef in the water since 2008, is home to flocks of black cormorants.
Sands drift into the hull of the Shawnee.
This ship’s origins and name are unknown, just one of hundreds of vessels to have crashed along the coast. A jackal’s footprints skirt the edge of the wreck.

“Whether that increase in power and opportunity ends up being more opportunity for mischief (or outright malfeasance), or opportunity to reclaim our civic life, might be up to how much we’re willing to pay attention and take back responsibility and control over the process,” said Michael Slaby, a former digital leader in Barack Obama’s presidential campaign and the chief strategist for Harmony Labs.
So as we gird for the next 12-plus months before Election Day
, I hope Tuesdays will serve as a road map through the digital morass. We’ll look at what the campaigns are doing smartly, or not so smartly, online. We’ll assess the spread, and sources, of misinformation. We’ll pick apart notable ads. And we’ll keep an eye on the ongoing effort to secure our elections.
So, even though it’s still early … buckle up.

The Buttigieg Campaign Finds a ‘Barrier’
Our colleague Trip Gabriel sends this report:
As Pete Buttigieg gains strength as a presidential candidate,
ticking upward in polls
and raking in donations, one continuing weakness is the cool reception he gets from black voters.
A little-discussed reason for that disconnect surfaced
Tuesday
in an internal campaign memo that was written by a consultant to the campaign. It said Mr. Buttigieg’s sexual orientation was a significant obstacle for African-American voters in South Carolina, an early-primary state where black voters make up a majority of the Democratic primary electorate.
Summarizing three focus groups of undecided black voters in the state, the memo concludes that “being gay was a barrier for these voters, particularly for the men who seemed deeply uncomfortable even discussing it.”
The focus groups were small and not statistically representative of the state’s electorate at large, to say nothing of black voters nationwide. But the memo sheds some light on how the Buttigieg campaign sees one of his biggest challenges in the primary.
Among 24 black voters ages 25 to 65 recruited by the Benenson Strategy Group in July, few had heard of Mr. Buttigieg, the 37-year-old mayor of South Bend, Ind. Although being gay was not necessarily a deal breaker, many of the voters feared it would make him unelectable against President Trump, according to
the memo
, which was first reported
by McClatchy
.
On learning about Mr. Buttigieg’s biography and record, several people seized on a single mention that he lives with his husband, complaining that he was flaunting being gay.
“That was too much information,” one woman said.
“I don’t like the fact that he threw out there that he lives with his husband,” a man said.
While many of the voters said they were not personally prejudiced, they said they believed that others, especially Republicans, would have problems with Mr. Buttigieg’s sexual orientation and that he would be a weak nominee.
“I don’t think he’s going to be able to be the one to bridge the gap,” a woman said. “I mean, it would be interesting, but it’s not going to happen.”
But there were also positive takeaways for the Buttigieg campaign. Once the voters learned more about the candidate, they scored him highly on his military service, his record in South Bend and his faith. And they were impressed when they heard him speak.
Mr. Buttigieg might raise his prospects among skeptical black voters, the consultant wrote, by winning “endorsements from ‘cool’ black people” to further the notion that being gay wouldn’t be a vulnerability in a face-off with Mr. Trump.
On the whole, the memo says that Mr. Buttigieg’s biggest problem with black voters — one he shares with other candidates — is simply that he is not former Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.
“The affinity these voters feel for Joe Biden is deep and strong, rooted in his relationship with Barack Obama who is the ultimate validator,” the memo states.
While Mr. Biden is struggling to hold off rivals in Iowa and New Hampshire, the first two states to vote next year, a
polling average in South Carolina
shows him with a 25-point lead.
A Digital Feast
Nick here, again. Often on Tuesdays, we’ll assess a noteworthy campaign ad in this space. But aside from all things messaging, I also really, really like to eat. Especially on the campaign trail.
So while I have your attention, I’ll occasionally be sharing the #campaignfoodreport, an Instagram series I started while covering the Trump campaign in 2016 with help from my colleague Jonathan Martin (and some other campaign road warriors like
NBC’s Ali Vitali
).
First up, with many of the 2020 candidates in Iowa this week, we’ll salivate over a Hawkeye State staple: the
loose meat sandwich
.
Also known as the tavern sandwich, the crumbly, greasy loose meat sandwich was first introduced as a “steamed hamburger” in Montana in 1920. Six years later, it migrated east, emerging as a “loose meat sandwich” at the original Maid-Rite fast food restaurant in Muscatine, Iowa. An institution was born.
With ground beef cooked crumbled (not molded into a patty), sizzled with a fistful of salt, onions and pepper, and smacked with yellow mustard, it’s as much a pulverized hamburger as it is a “sloppy joe without the slop.” The fatty concoction is cut with some sweet pickles.
Along with the Maid-Rite version, perhaps the most famous loose meat sandwich can be found under a parking garage in Ottumwa, Iowa, where the
Canteen Lunch restaurant
has been piling them high since 1936. The squat, yellow building served as the inspiration for the “Lanford Lunch Box” on the sitcom “Roseanne.”
Earlier this month, I traversed Iowa tracking down the
80-plus family members of Senator Cory Booker
scattered around the state. One night,
with my dining options hobbled by an hourlong Booker selfie line that began at 8:30 p.m.
, I decamped to the basement of the St. Burch Tavern in Iowa City, where a Green Goddess salad helped assuage the guilt of my second loose meat sandwich of the week.
Loose meat sandwiches can be found all over the Midwest, but sadly, not anywhere near The New York Times’s headquarters. Yet.

Barbara Low, who was among a core of female scientists whose research in the 1940s unleashed a bonanza of lifesaving antibiotics, and whose gumption gained her followers a foothold in a male-dominated field, died on Jan. 10 at her home in the Riverdale section of the Bronx. She was 98.
Her death was confirmed by Lucky Tran, a spokesman for the Irving Medical Center of Columbia University, where Dr. Low taught for nearly 60 years and was professor emeritus of biochemistry and molecular physics. Her death was announced belatedly because it took time for the university to gather biographical details, Ms. Tran said.
Dr. Low’s role in identifying the structure of penicillin was something of a fluke.
As a student at Oxford University in England, she was a protégé of the future Nobel laureate
Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin
, who, having been barred from teaching men, taught at Oxford’s
Somerville College
, a women’s school at the time.
At Somerville, Professor Hodgkin was a founder of protein crystallography, a process that can determine a molecule’s three-dimensional shape by analyzing how X-rays bend and bounce off its crystallized form. She trained a cadre of students, including Barbara Low, in the emerging field.
“Red-hot news,” Dr. Low told Professor Hodgkin in July 1943, according to the book “Dorothy Hodgkin: A Life” (2014), by Georgina Ferry. “Penicillin and all its degradation products contain sulfur. This is very hush-hush.”
Their wartime research helped transform penicillin — the bacteria-killing substance that Alexander Fleming had discovered in mold in 1928 — into a wonder drug that could be replicated, mass-produced and reconfigured to produce stronger antibiotic derivatives for the treatment of a broader range of infections.
Professor Hodgkin had begun her career in 1932 in the laboratory of
John Desmond Bernal
, a pioneer in X-ray crystallography, at the University of Cambridge in England. At Oxford, she and Dr. Low focused on penicillin, which was first used to treat humans in 1941.
Chemists were still attempting to isolate pure penicillin so it could be studied and synthesized. They used rudimentary computers. But as
Ernst B. Chain
, their colleague at Oxford, later said, “The final solution of the problem of the structure of penicillin came from crystallographic X-ray studies.”
Professor Hodgkin received the
Nobel Prize in Chemistry
in 1964 for her breakthrough research in crystallography. The award citation went beyond her work in penicillin to mention her subsequent determination of the crystal structure of vitamin B-12 and other substances that proved vital in advancing medical care.
Barbara Wharton Low was born on March 23, 1920, in Lancaster, in northwestern England, to Matthew and Mary Jane (Wharton) Low. She graduated from Sommerville with a bachelor’s degree in chemistry in 1943 and later received her master’s and doctorate in chemistry from Oxford.
After emigrating to the United States (she became a citizen in 1956), she was a research assistant to
Linus C. Pauling
, another future Nobel laureate, at the California Institute of Technology, and to the biochemist Edwin Cohn at Harvard. In 1950 she was appointed an assistant professor of biophysical chemistry at Harvard, where she discovered a protein structural element in amino acids known as the pi helix.
Dr. Low joined the Columbia faculty as an associate professor in 1956 and was promoted to professor in 1966. Her research there led to a better understanding of the protein receptor that responds to the neurotransmitter targeted by snake venom.
She retired as a professor in 1990, but she continued to lecture at the university until 2013.
Her legacy at Columbia went beyond academics: It was grounded in a commitment to rectify the second-class treatment her mentor had received as a teacher at Oxford.
“On the university’s affirmative action committee, she was very forceful in wanting Columbia to live up to its ideals of having a diverse faculty and work force,” Arthur G. Palmer, a professor of biochemistry and molecular biophysics and associate dean for graduate affairs at Columbia’s medical center, said in an email.
In 1950 Dr. Low married Metchie J. E. Budka, a fellow biochemist whom she had met at Harvard. He died in 1995. A sister, Marjorie Elizabeth Camp, died in 2002. No immediate family members survive.
